activities.title: Fix Tavon's Van Count
activities.instructions:
1. Students read Tavon's work and underline the exact operation he chose.
2. They draw 5 vans and deal 8 students into each to see what the total really is.
3. They rewrite the check as multiplication and re-judge the statement.
4. Share out: why does 'per van' mean multiply, never add?

content.worked_problem: Given: 1 van carries 8 students. Statement: '5 vans carry 40 students.' Tavon wrote 5 + 8 = 13 and marked the statement FALSE.
content.error_step: Tavon added the number of vans to the unit rate.
content.why: Each of the 5 vans carries its own 8 students — five groups of 8 is 5 x 8 = 40. The statement is true; addition merges the two numbers instead of copying the rate per unit.

activities.title: True Rate / False Rate
materials: Statement deck (one unit rate + 5 statements per round)
activities.instructions:
1. Reveal a unit rate card: 'A machine makes 5 bracelets per hour.'
2. Flip statement cards one at a time ('4 hours makes 9 bracelets'). Everyone computes the TRUE amount on their whiteboard before voting true/false.
3. Score a point only if your written math supports your vote.
4. Rotate a 'trap-maker': after each round, that student invents the next false statement — it must use addition or a wrong rate to be tempting.
5. Debrief: which trap fooled the most people and why?

strategy_links.why: Quick 'compute 4 x 6 in your head and defend it' talks build the multiplicative reflex the addition error replaces.
The add-instead-of-multiply statement is a perfect find-and-fix: the drawn groups instantly expose 5 + 8.
Whiteboard votes with the check-math showing reveal who judges statements by feel instead of computing.

questioning_prompts: Before you judge the statement — what does YOUR math say the true amount is?
What does 'per' promise about each unit?
If 1 pizza feeds 4, walk me up: 2 pizzas feed...? 3 pizzas feed...? What's the pattern doing?
The statement is false. What exact mistake would make someone write it?
How could you use the same rate to check a statement about 100 units without counting up?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student adds the unit rate to the unit count — says 3 pizzas feed 7 people when 1 feeds 4.
misconception_redirects.say: Say the rate as 'EACH pizza feeds 4.' Now count it out: 1 pizza feeds 4, 2 pizzas feed 8, 3 pizzas feed... Each new pizza brings its own 4, so the operation is multiplication. Redo the statement with units x rate.
misconception_redirects.praise: You gave every unit its own copy of the rate — that's what 'per' means.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student judges statements by gut ('20 sounds like a lot for 5 pizzas') without computing.
misconception_redirects.say: No verdict until there's math on the page. Write units x rate, get YOUR number, then compare it to the statement's number.
misconception_redirects.praise: Compute first, judge second — that's how you never get tricked.

quick_checks.prompt: 1 shelf holds 9 books. Do 6 shelves hold 15 books or 54 books?
quick_checks.look_for: 54 with '6 x 9.' Choosing 15 diagnoses the addition merge (6 + 9).

quick_checks.prompt: Make up the NEXT true statement: 1 hour of babysitting pays $8, so 2 hours pay $16, 3 hours pay...
quick_checks.look_for: $24, continuing the multiplicative pattern. Saying $17 or $18 signals adding 8 once then drifting.

sentence_starters: Each unit brings its own ___, so I multiplied ___ x ___.
The statement says ___, but my math says ___, so it is ___.

worked_solution.stem: A pizza restaurant advertises that 1 large pizza will feed 4 people. Is this statement true: '5 pizzas will feed 20 people'? What about '3 pizzas will feed 6 people'?
worked_solution.answer: '5 pizzas feed 20' is true; '3 pizzas feed 6' is false (they feed 12).

steps.annotation: 'Per 1' is the anchor — every pizza brings its own 4 people.
Compute the true amount BEFORE judging. 20 matches the claim — TRUE.
The claim says 6. Our math says 12 — FALSE.
Name the trap: the false statement added or doubled instead of using the rate. Compute, then judge.

faded_example.stem: A garden hose fills 3 gallons per minute. Test the statement: '7 minutes will fill 21 gallons.'

steps.annotation: Anchor on the per-1 amount.
Each minute adds its own 3 gallons — multiplication.
Compute 7 x 3.
Compare your number to the statement's 21 and give the verdict.

skills.name: Calculate a unit rate from a real-world rate and use it
skills.i_do_script: This is the full round trip. A runner does 6 laps in 42 minutes. Step one, find the unit rate: 42 minutes divided by 6 laps is 7 — it takes 7 minutes per lap. Step two, USE it: how long for 10 laps? 10 x 7 = 70 minutes. Two moves every time — divide down to 1, then multiply up to whatever the question asks. The only decision is which number gets divided by which, and the units in the question tell you: 'minutes per lap' means minutes get divided by laps.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides the two quantities in whichever order the story lists them, instead of the order the requested unit rate demands
canonical_error.example: For '6 laps in 42 minutes — find minutes per lap,' student computes 6 / 42 = 1/7 instead of 42 / 6 = 7
canonical_error.why: The student pulls numbers in story order rather than reading the unit phrase. 'Minutes per lap' names the division — the unit before 'per' goes on top (gets divided by the other) — and without that anchor the division direction is a coin flip.

skills.item_template: A real-world rate with compatible whole numbers ('6 laps in 42 minutes'). Part A: find the requested unit rate (units named). Part B: multiply the unit rate to answer a scaled question. Two-part numeric response.

sample_items.stem:
A person runs 6 laps around a track in 42 minutes.

What is the rate, in minutes, in which the person runs one lap?

___ minutes per lap
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1/7 (about 0.14) signals dividing 6 / 42 in story order; 36 signals subtracting; 252 signals multiplying

sample_items.stem:
A bakery uses 48 cups of flour to make 8 batches of muffins.

Part A: How many cups of flour are used for 1 batch?

Part B: How many cups of flour are needed for 13 batches?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Part A of 1/6 signals story-order division (8 / 48); Part B of 19 signals adding 13 + 6 instead of multiplying

sample_items.stem:
A worker earns $91 for 7 hours of work.

Part A: How much does the worker earn per hour?

Part B: At that rate, how much will the worker earn for 20 hours?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Part A of $84 signals subtracting; Part B of $33 signals adding 20 + 13; $273 signals using 21 hours

sample_items.stem:
A train traveling at a constant speed covers 180 miles in 4 hours.

Part A: What is the train's speed in miles per hour?

Part B: How far does the train travel in 9 hours?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Part A of 1/45 signals hours / miles; Part B of 54 signals adding 9 + 45; 176 signals subtracting

redirect_script.stop: Pause — read the units in the question again.
redirect_script.prompt: The question says 'minutes per lap.' Underline the unit BEFORE 'per' — that's the one being divided. Say it as a sentence: 'minutes divided by laps.' Now match each number to its unit and set up the division.
redirect_script.praise: You let the units choose the division — that's the move that never fails.

vocabulary.definition: How much of one quantity goes with exactly 1 of the other, like 7 minutes per 1 lap.
The word that names the division — 'miles per hour' means miles divided by hours.
A rate that stays the same the whole time, so scaling up is safe.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'A person runs 6 laps in 42 minutes. What is the rate in minutes per lap?'
Two numbers, two units. Before dividing anything — which unit does the question put BEFORE the word 'per'?
'Minutes per lap' is an instruction: minutes divided by laps. The unit before 'per' is the one that gets divided.
Label the numbers: 42 MINUTES, 6 LAPS. Set up 42 / 6 and solve: 7.
Say the answer as a full rate sentence. 7 WHAT per WHAT? Does '7 minutes per lap' sound right for a runner?
If the student sets up 6 / 42 because 6 came first in the story, don't correct — ask them to compute it (about 0.14) and check it against sense: 'Could one lap really take a seventh of a minute?'
Now USE the rate: at 7 minutes per lap, how long would 10 laps take? Which operation, and why?
Your turn, both steps: a printer makes 96 copies in 8 minutes. Find copies per minute, then predict copies in 15 minutes.

practice_problems.stem: $24 for 4 pounds of cheese. What is the price per pound?
practice_problems.answer: $6 per pound

practice_problems.stem: At 9 miles per hour, how far do you bike in 3 hours?
practice_problems.answer: 27 miles

practice_problems.stem: A person runs 5 laps in 40 minutes. Part A: minutes per lap? Part B: at that rate, how long for 12 laps?
practice_problems.answer: Part A: 8 minutes per lap (40 / 5); Part B: 96 minutes (12 x 8).
practice_problems.notes: The full round trip: divide down to 1, multiply up.

practice_problems.stem: A factory fills 72 bottles in 6 minutes. Find bottles per minute, then bottles in 25 minutes.
practice_problems.answer: 12 bottles per minute (72 / 6); 300 bottles (25 x 12).
practice_problems.notes: Watch the division direction — 'bottles per minute' puts bottles on top.

practice_problems.stem: Lena found a unit rate. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Problem: A cyclist rides 8 miles in 56 minutes. Find the minutes per mile.
practice_problems.answer: Lena divided in story order — miles first — but 'minutes per mile' says minutes get divided by miles: 56 / 8 = 7 minutes per mile. Her answer fails the sense check too: a mile can't take a seventh of a minute.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error with fresh numbers: story-order division instead of unit-phrase division.

practice_problems.stem: Ground beef costs $18 for 3 pounds at Store A and $28 for 4 pounds at Store B. Which store has the cheaper price per pound?
practice_problems.answer: Store A — $6 per pound (18 / 3) vs $7 per pound (28 / 4).
practice_problems.notes: Comparing rates is the payoff of scaling both to 1.

practice_problems.stem: A car travels 15 miles in 20 minutes. Find the rate in miles per MINUTE (careful — it isn't a whole number), then use it to find miles per hour.
practice_problems.answer: 0.75 miles per minute (15 / 20); 45 miles per hour (0.75 x 60).
practice_problems.notes: Non-whole unit rate plus a unit conversion — the divide-then-multiply structure survives both.

practice_problems.stem: Write a rate story whose unit rate is 12, where the story lists the numbers in REVERSE order of the division (the divisor first).
practice_problems.answer: Sample: 'In 4 hours the crew painted 48 fence panels — find panels per hour.' The 4 appears first but 48 / 4 = 12.
practice_problems.notes: The spec's 'difficult' twist: quantities presented in reverse order of the expected unit rate.

activities.title: Story, Division, Rate
activities.instructions:
1. Match each rate story to the division that finds its unit rate. Two division cards are decoys — they divide in story order instead of unit order.
2. To claim a match, read the unit phrase aloud and point at which number lands on top.
3. Debrief: what one word in the question tells you the division direction?

pairs.left: 6 laps in 42 minutes -- minutes per lap
96 pages in 8 days -- pages per day
5 hours to mow 40 lawns -- lawns per hour
120 miles on 4 gallons -- miles per gallon

activities.title: Two-Step Rate Relay
materials: Problem strips with a rate and a scaled question
activities.instructions:
1. Partner A does step one only: find the unit rate and write it as a labeled sentence ('13 dollars per 1 hour').
2. Partner B takes over for step two: use A's unit rate to answer the scaled question ('how much for 20 hours?').
3. B must check A's direction before building on it — if A divided the wrong way, B sends it back with the unit phrase underlined.
4. Swap roles each strip. Debrief: which step hides more mistakes, and why?

activities.title: Best Deal Showdown
materials: Deck of price cards ('$32 for 4 pizzas', '$45 for 5 pizzas')
activities.instructions:
1. Flip two price cards for the same item.
2. Both partners race to find each card's price per 1 item, showing the division on the whiteboard.
3. The pair must agree which is the better deal and say the comparison sentence: '___ per 1 beats ___ per 1.'
4. Trap rounds: some cards list the count before the price ('4 hours for $52') — the unit phrase, not the story order, picks the division.
5. Debrief: why does scaling both prices to 1 make the comparison fair?

strategy_links.why: The division-direction decision is invisible — thinking aloud ('minutes per lap, so minutes on top') externalizes it.
The two-move routine (divide to 1, multiply up) is ideal for I Do / We Do / You Do release.
Story-order division produces absurd rates (1/7 minute per lap) — sense-checking flawed work builds the reflex.

questioning_prompts: Which unit comes before 'per' in the question? So which number gets divided?
Say your answer as a full sentence with both units. Does it make sense in the real world?
You found the unit rate — what does the question want you to DO with it now?
Why do we bother scaling to 1 first instead of jumping straight to 13 batches?
If your Part A were wrong, what would happen to Part B? How could you catch that?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides in story order — computes 6 / 42 for 'minutes per lap' because the 6 came first.
misconception_redirects.say: The question says 'minutes per lap.' Underline the unit BEFORE 'per' — that's the one being divided. Say it as a sentence: 'minutes divided by laps.' Now match each number to its unit and set up the division.
misconception_redirects.praise: You let the units choose the division — that's the move that never fails.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student finds the unit rate correctly in Part A, then ADDS it to the scale factor in Part B (7 + 10 instead of 7 x 10).
misconception_redirects.say: Part A says every lap costs 7 minutes. If you run 10 laps, each one brings its own 7 — is that adding one 7, or ten 7s?
misconception_redirects.praise: You multiplied the rate by the count — every lap paid its own 7 minutes.

quick_checks.prompt: $36 for 4 movie tickets — price per ticket, in one line.
quick_checks.look_for: $9 via 36 / 4. An answer of 1/9 or 0.11 diagnoses story-order division; 32 diagnoses subtraction.

quick_checks.prompt: You know a pool fills at 15 gallons per minute. How much in 6 minutes — and which operation did you just use?
quick_checks.look_for: 90 gallons, named as multiplication. Hesitation between x and / on the scaling step means the round trip isn't automatic yet.

sentence_starters: The question says ___ per ___, so I divided ___ by ___.
One ___ takes ___, so ___ of them take ___ x ___.

worked_solution.stem: A person runs 6 laps around a track in 42 minutes. Part A: What is the rate in minutes per lap? Part B: At that rate, how long will 10 laps take?
worked_solution.answer: Part A: 7 minutes per lap; Part B: 70 minutes

steps.annotation: The unit before 'per' gets divided. The question, not the story order, picks the direction.
Divide down to 1. Sense check: 7 minutes for a lap is believable; 6/42 of a minute is not.
Use the rate: every lap brings its own 7 minutes, so multiply.
Dividing the answer back by the laps returns the unit rate — the round trip closes.

faded_example.stem: A store sells 5 pounds of apples for $35. Part A: What is the price per pound? Part B: How much would 9 pounds cost?
faded_example.answer: Part A: $7 per pound; Part B: $63

steps.annotation: The unit before 'per' is the one divided.
Divide down to 1.
Part B: each pound costs $7 — compute 9 x 7.
Check: divide your Part B answer by 9. Do you get the unit rate back?

skills.name: Critique and correct flawed unit-rate reasoning
skills.i_do_script: Now you become the teacher. A student wrote: 'A car travels 120 miles in 2 hours. Speed = 2 hours / 120 miles = 1/60 miles per hour.' My critique routine has three checks: (1) UNITS — the question wants miles per hour, so miles must be divided by hours; this student flipped it. (2) ARITHMETIC — 2/120 does equal 1/60, so the arithmetic isn't the bug. (3) SENSE — could a car really go 1/60 of a mile in an hour? Never. A full critique names the error, explains it, and shows the fix: 120 / 2 = 60 miles per hour.

canonical_error.pattern: Critiques only the arithmetic and declares flipped-rate work 'correct' because the computation checks out
canonical_error.example: Reviewing 'speed = 2 / 120 = 1/60 mph,' student verifies that 2/120 reduces to 1/60 and concludes there is no error
canonical_error.why: The student equates 'checked' with 'recomputed.' They audit the calculation but never audit the SETUP — whether the right quantity was divided by the right one — so an error that lives in the setup passes their inspection untouched.

skills.item_template: A worked solution to a rate problem containing a setup error (usually an inverted division). Student identifies the error, explains why it's wrong, and provides the corrected unit rate. Constructed response with a numeric correction.

sample_items.stem:
A student solved the given problem.

Problem: A car travels 120 miles in 2 hours. What is its speed in miles per hour?

Solution: Speed = 2 hours/120 miles = 1/60 miles per hour

Identify and explain the error the student made in solving the problem. Provide the correct solution.
sample_items.answer: The rate is flipped — 'miles per hour' means miles divided by hours, so time belongs in the denominator. Correct: 120 miles / 2 hours = 60 miles per hour.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who only recheck arithmetic will accept 2/120 = 1/60 and miss the inverted setup; some will 'fix' it to 60 without naming the error

sample_items.stem:
A student solved the given problem.

Problem: A swimmer completes 96 laps in 12 hours of practice. How many laps does she swim per hour?

Solution: 12 / 96 = 1/8 lap per hour

Identify and explain the error the student made. Provide the correct solution.
sample_items.answer: The division is inverted — 'laps per hour' puts laps on top: 96 / 12 = 8 laps per hour. 1/8 of a lap per hour fails the sense check for a swimmer at practice.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Accepting the work because 12/96 does reduce to 1/8 signals arithmetic-only checking

sample_items.stem:
A student solved the given problem.

Problem: A store sells 15 pounds of dog food for $45. What is the price per pound?

Solution: 15 / 45 = 1/3, so the food costs about $0.33 per pound

Identify and explain the error. Provide the correct price per pound.
sample_items.answer: The student divided pounds by dollars. 'Dollars per pound' means 45 / 15 = $3 per pound. The arithmetic 15/45 = 1/3 is right, but it answers a different question (pounds per dollar).
sample_items.distractor_logic: The flipped answer is a true statement about pounds per dollar — students must catch that it answers the wrong question, not that it computes wrong

sample_items.stem:
A student solved the given problem.

Problem: A plane flies 1,500 miles in 3 hours. What is its speed in miles per hour?

Solution: 1500 x 3 = 4,500 miles per hour

Identify and explain the error the student made. Provide the correct solution.
sample_items.answer: The student multiplied instead of dividing. Finding a per-hour amount from 3 hours means splitting: 1500 / 3 = 500 miles per hour. 4,500 mph also fails the sense check — the plane would be faster than any jet.
sample_items.distractor_logic: A different setup bug (wrong operation, not inversion) — checks that the critique routine generalizes beyond 'flip it'

redirect_script.stop: You checked the math — now check the setup.
redirect_script.prompt: Run all three checks out loud: UNITS — what does the question put before 'per,' and is that what got divided? ARITHMETIC — does the computation itself work? SENSE — could that answer happen in real life? An error can hide in any of the three.
redirect_script.praise: You caught an error the calculator can't see — that's setup-level thinking.

vocabulary.definition: Examining someone's work to find and explain exactly where it goes wrong.
The plan of the calculation — which numbers, which operation, which order — before any arithmetic happens.
Asking whether an answer could really happen in the situation, like a car going 1/60 of a mile per hour.
Giving the reason your correction is right, not just the new answer.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 7.RP.2 — constant of proportionality and proportional relationships.

worked_example_script.text: Post the flawed work: 'Problem: A car travels 120 miles in 2 hours. What is its speed in miles per hour? Solution: Speed = 2 hours / 120 miles = 1/60 miles per hour.'
We're grading this like a teacher. Three checks, always in this order: units, arithmetic, sense.
Check one — UNITS. The question asks for miles per hour. In the student's fraction, what got divided by what?
Check two — ARITHMETIC. Is 2/120 really 1/60? So is the arithmetic the problem here, or not?
This is the trap moment: many students see correct arithmetic and declare the work fine. If that happens, push to check three instead of correcting.
Check three — SENSE. A car drives for an hour and covers 1/60 of a mile. Could that be right? What does that tell you about where the error lives?
The error is in the SETUP: the rate is flipped. 'Miles per hour' means miles divided by hours — 120 / 2 = 60 miles per hour. A full critique says all three things: what's wrong, why, and the fix.
Your turn to grade: 'A baker frosts 45 cupcakes in 9 minutes. Rate = 9 / 45 = 1/5 cupcake per minute.' Run the three checks and write the full critique.

practice_problems.stem: The question asks for 'pages per minute.' Which quantity goes in the denominator?
practice_problems.answer: minutes

practice_problems.stem: Sense check only: could '2 miles per hour' be a walking speed? Could '1/50 mile per hour' be a car's highway speed?
practice_problems.answer: Yes — 2 mph is a normal walk. No — 1/50 mph is far too slow for a car; a flipped setup is likely.

practice_problems.stem: Grade this work: 'A hose fills 80 gallons in 16 minutes. Rate = 16 / 80 = 1/5 gallon per minute.' Name the error, explain it, and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: Inverted setup — 'gallons per minute' means 80 / 16 = 5 gallons per minute. The arithmetic was fine; the division direction was not.
practice_problems.notes: The full three-part critique: name, explain, fix.

practice_problems.stem: Priya CHECKED a classmate's work. Find the mistake in Priya's checking.
shown_work: Classmate's work: 'A bus travels 150 miles in 3 hours. Speed = 3 / 150 = 1/50 mile per hour.'
Priya wrote: 'I checked: 3 divided by 150 really is 1/50. The work is correct.'
practice_problems.answer: Priya only audited the arithmetic. The setup is flipped: 'miles per hour' requires 150 / 3 = 50 miles per hour. Correct arithmetic on a wrong setup is still a wrong answer — and 1/50 mph fails the sense check.
practice_problems.notes: The canonical error, one level up: a flawed critique of flawed work.

practice_problems.stem: Grade this work: 'Tickets are $8 each. For 6 tickets: 8 + 6 = $14.' Name the error, explain it, and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: Wrong operation — each ticket costs its own $8, so 6 tickets cost 6 x 8 = $48. Addition merged the count with the rate.
practice_problems.notes: Setup errors aren't always inversions — the routine must catch wrong operations too.

practice_problems.stem: Two students found the unit rate for '210 miles on 10 gallons.' Ava: 210 / 10 = 21 miles per gallon. Ben: 10 / 210 = 1/21 gallon per mile. Who answered 'miles per gallon,' and is the other one WRONG or just answering a different question?
practice_problems.answer: Ava answered miles per gallon (21). Ben's number is actually a true rate — gallons per mile — but it does not answer the question asked. Both critiques matter: setup must match the question.
practice_problems.notes: Subtle: the flipped rate is true information aimed at the wrong target.

practice_problems.stem: Write your own flawed solution to 'A runner covers 24 miles in 4 hours — find miles per hour,' hiding the error in the SETUP while keeping the arithmetic perfect. Trade and critique.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: 'Speed = 4 / 24 = 1/6 mile per hour' — arithmetic is flawless, setup is inverted. The fix: 24 / 4 = 6 miles per hour.
practice_problems.notes: Designing the trap is the deepest form of owning it.

practice_problems.stem: A student claims: 'Any rate problem can be checked just by re-doing the division on a calculator.' Write two or three sentences arguing for or against, using an example.
practice_problems.answer: Against — a calculator re-verifies arithmetic but can't see whether the setup matches the question. Example: 2 / 120 = 1/60 checks out perfectly, yet 'speed = 1/60 mph' is wrong because miles per hour needs 120 / 2.
practice_problems.notes: Names the meta-lesson of the whole skill.

activities.title: Grade the Grader
materials: Printed slip with the bus problem and Priya's check (below)
activities.instructions:
1. Partners read the classmate's work AND Priya's check of it.
2. First pass: run the three checks (units, arithmetic, sense) on the classmate's work and write where the error lives.
3. Second pass: say exactly what Priya's checking routine was missing.
4. Write the full correction with units labeled.
5. Debrief question: why can a solution with perfect arithmetic still be wrong?

content.worked_problem: Classmate: 'A bus travels 150 miles in 3 hours. Speed = 3 / 150 = 1/50 mile per hour.' Priya's check: '3 divided by 150 is 1/50 — correct!'
content.error_step: The classmate inverted the division; Priya audited only the arithmetic and blessed the flipped setup.
content.why: 'Miles per hour' fixes the setup: miles divided by hours, 150 / 3 = 50 mph. Arithmetic checking can never catch a setup error — only the units and sense checks can.

activities.title: Where Does the Error Live?
activities.instructions:
1. Header cards: Setup error, Arithmetic error, No error.
2. The group sorts each worked solution, running the three checks aloud.
3. Rule: a card can't land until someone states the fix (or, for 'No error,' restates why it survives all three checks).
4. Debrief: which pile was hardest to spot, and which check caught it?

cards.text: 60 pages in 5 days: 60 x 5 = 300 pages per day
84 laps in 7 days: 84 / 7 = 14 laps per day
72 beads on 8 strings: 8 / 72 = 1/9 bead per string

activities.title: Sabotage
materials: A list of clean rate problems
activities.instructions:
1. Each partner takes a clean problem ('A kayaker paddles 18 miles in 3 hours — find mph') and secretly writes a WRONG solution, choosing where to hide the bug: setup or arithmetic.
2. Trade papers. The critic must (a) find the error, (b) name which kind it is, (c) fix it — one point for each.
3. Bonus point to the saboteur if the critic mislabels the error's location.
4. Two rounds each. Debrief: which errors were hardest to hide, and which check exposed them?

strategy_links.why: The skill IS worked-example-plus-error-analysis — pairing a correct solution beside the flipped one makes the setup difference visible.
Critiques improve when rehearsed aloud: partners must convince each other where the error lives before writing.
Modeling the three-check routine (units, arithmetic, sense) as a think-aloud gives students a script for auditing setup, not just computation.

questioning_prompts: Where does the error live — the setup or the arithmetic? How do you know?
The question says 'miles per hour.' What did the student actually divide?
Does the answer survive a sense check? Could that number happen in real life?
The student's arithmetic is perfect. Can the answer still be wrong? Why?
Your critique names the error — now what's the fix, with units?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student recomputes the arithmetic, finds it correct, and declares flipped-rate work 'fine.'
misconception_redirects.say: Run all three checks out loud: UNITS — what does the question put before 'per,' and is that what got divided? ARITHMETIC — does the computation itself work? SENSE — could that answer happen in real life? An error can hide in any of the three.
misconception_redirects.praise: You caught an error the calculator can't see — that's setup-level thinking.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student jumps straight to the right answer ('it's 60') without naming or explaining the error.
misconception_redirects.say: Half credit so far — the problem asks you to identify and EXPLAIN the error. Point at the student's fraction and tell me what they divided and what they should have divided.
misconception_redirects.praise: Now that's a full critique: the error, the why, and the fix.

quick_checks.prompt: In one sentence: what's wrong with 'speed = 2 hours / 120 miles'?
quick_checks.look_for: 'The rate is flipped — miles belong on top / time in the denominator.' A student who says 'nothing, 2/120 = 1/60' is auditing arithmetic only.

quick_checks.prompt: Name the three checks in order.
quick_checks.look_for: Units, arithmetic, sense. Missing 'units' predicts they'll keep blessing inverted setups.

sentence_starters: The error is in the ___ because the question asks for ___ per ___.
The arithmetic is ___, but the setup should be ___ divided by ___.

worked_solution.stem: A student solved: 'A car travels 120 miles in 2 hours. What is its speed in miles per hour?' Solution: 'Speed = 2 hours / 120 miles = 1/60 miles per hour.' Identify and explain the error, then give the correct solution.
worked_solution.answer: The rate is flipped; correct speed = 120 / 2 = 60 miles per hour.

steps.math: check UNITS: 'miles per hour' -> miles / hours
steps.annotation: The question fixes the setup: miles on top, hours in the denominator. The student wrote hours / miles — flipped.
The computation itself has no bug — which is exactly why arithmetic-only checking misses this error.

steps.math: check SENSE: 1/60 mile in an hour?
steps.annotation: A car covering 1/60 of a mile per hour is absurd — confirmation the setup is wrong.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S5, calculating a unit rate from a real-world rate and using it, the At-proficiency core. If they pass, move up to S6, critiquing flawed rate reasoning. If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks multi-digit division and B2 checks reading a fraction as division with a decimal answer, the two grade 5 skills every unit-rate division leans on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (division facts within 100) and F2 (decimal notation for tenths and hundredths) locate the gap in grades 3 and 4. S1 through S4 remain available to probe the standard's own recognize, scale, and model work.
